sections.title: Overview
sections.body:
**Project 14:** TEXT CLASSIFICATION (NLP BASICS)

**What you'll learn:**
- Text preprocessing for ML
- CountVectorizer (Bag of Words)
- TF-IDF (Term Frequency - Inverse Document Frequency)
- How text becomes numbers for ML models
- Text classification pipeline
- Comparing BoW vs TF-IDF

**Dataset:** 20 Newsgroups (sklearn built-in)
- Text documents from 20 newsgroups
- We'll use 4 categories for simplicity

**Type:** MULTI-CLASS TEXT CLASSIFICATION

sections.title: Step 1: Understand Text → Numbers
sections.body:
```python
text_intro = """
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║              HOW TEXT BECOMES NUMBERS FOR ML                         ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                      ║
║  ML models need NUMBERS, not text. How to convert?                   ║
║                                                                      ║
║  METHOD 1: CountVectorizer (Bag of Words)                            ║
║  ─────────────────────────────────────────                           ║
║  "I love ML" → count each word                                      ║
║  Vocabulary: [I, love, ML, hate, data]                               ║
║  "I love ML"   → [1, 1, 1, 0, 0]                                    ║
║  "I hate ML"   → [1, 0, 1, 1, 0]                                    ║
║  "I love data" → [1, 1, 0, 0, 1]                                    ║
║                                                                      ║
║  PROBLEM: Common words like "the", "is" get high counts              ║
║  but carry NO meaning!                                               ║
║                                                                      ║
║  METHOD 2: TF-IDF (Term Frequency × Inverse Document Frequency)      ║
║  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────             ║
║  TF:  How often word appears in THIS document                        ║
║  IDF: How RARE the word is across ALL documents                      ║
║  TF-IDF = TF × IDF                                                  ║
║                                                                      ║
║  Words in MANY docs → low IDF → low TF-IDF (less important)         ║
║  Words in FEW docs → high IDF → high TF-IDF (more important!)       ║
║                                                                      ║
║  Example:                                                            ║
║  "the" → appears everywhere → low TF-IDF                            ║
║  "neural" → rare, specific → high TF-IDF                            ║
║                                                                      ║
║  TF-IDF is almost always BETTER than raw counts!                     ║
║                                                                      ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
"""
print(text_intro)
```

sections.title: Step 2: Load Data
sections.body:
```python
# Use 4 distinct categories for clarity
categories = ["sci.space", "rec.sport.baseball", "comp.graphics", "talk.politics.guns"]

train_data = fetch_20newsgroups(
    subset="train",
    categories=categories,
    remove=("headers", "footers", "quotes"),
    random_state=42,
)
test_data = fetch_20newsgroups(
    subset="test",
    categories=categories,
    remove=("headers", "footers", "quotes"),
    random_state=42,
)

X_train_text = train_data.data
y_train = train_data.target
X_test_text = test_data.data
y_test = test_data.target
target_names = train_data.target_names

print(f"Training documents: {len(X_train_text)}")
print(f"Test documents: {len(X_test_text)}")
print(f"Categories: {target_names}")
print(f"\nClass distribution (train):")
for i, name in enumerate(target_names):
    count = sum(y_train == i)
    print(f"  {name}: {count} ({count/len(y_train):.1%})")

# Show sample documents
print(f"\n{'='*50}")
print("SAMPLE DOCUMENTS:")
print(f"{'='*50}")
for i in range(3):
    print(f"\n--- Category: {target_names[y_train[i]]} ---")
    text = X_train_text[i][:200].strip()
    print(f"{text}...")
```

sections.title: Step 3: CountVectorizer (Bag of Words)
sections.body:
```python
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("METHOD 1: CountVectorizer (Bag of Words)")
print("=" * 60)

# Basic CountVectorizer
count_vec = CountVectorizer(
    max_features=10000,  # Keep top 10K words
    stop_words="english",  # Remove "the", "is", "a", etc.
    min_df=2,  # Word must appear in ≥2 documents
    max_df=0.95,  # Ignore words in >95% of documents
)

X_train_count = count_vec.fit_transform(X_train_text)
X_test_count = count_vec.transform(X_test_text)

print(f"Vocabulary size: {len(count_vec.vocabulary_)}")
print(f"Feature matrix shape: {X_train_count.shape}")
print(f"Matrix type: {type(X_train_count).__name__} (sparse!)")
print(
    f"Sparsity: {1 - X_train_count.nnz / (X_train_count.shape[0] * X_train_count.shape[1]):.1%}"
)

# Show top words
feature_names = count_vec.get_feature_names_out()
word_counts = X_train_count.sum(axis=0).A1
top_words = pd.Series(word_counts, index=feature_names).nlargest(20)
print(f"\nTop 20 words:\n{top_words}")
```

sections.title: Step 4: Tf-Idf Vectorizer
sections.body:
```python
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("METHOD 2: TF-IDF Vectorizer")
print("=" * 60)

tfidf_vec = TfidfVectorizer(
    max_features=10000,
    stop_words="english",
    min_df=2,
    max_df=0.95,
    ngram_range=(1, 2),  # unigrams + bigrams!
    sublinear_tf=True,  # Use log(1 + tf) instead of tf
)

X_train_tfidf = tfidf_vec.fit_transform(X_train_text)
X_test_tfidf = tfidf_vec.transform(X_test_text)

print(f"TF-IDF features: {X_train_tfidf.shape[1]}")
print(f"(includes bigrams like 'machine learning', 'neural network')")

# Top TF-IDF words per category
print(f"\nTop TF-IDF words per category:")
tfidf_features = tfidf_vec.get_feature_names_out()
for cat_idx, cat_name in enumerate(target_names):
    cat_mask = y_train == cat_idx
    mean_tfidf = X_train_tfidf[cat_mask].mean(axis=0).A1
    top_idx = mean_tfidf.argsort()[-8:][::-1]
    top_words_cat = [tfidf_features[i] for i in top_idx]
    print(f"  {cat_name}: {', '.join(top_words_cat)}")
```

sections.title: Step 5: Compare Models
sections.body:
```python
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("MODEL COMPARISON: CountVectorizer vs TF-IDF")
print("=" * 60)

models = {
    "Naive Bayes": MultinomialNB(),
    "Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=42),
    "Linear SVM": LinearSVC(random_state=42, max_iter=5000),
}

print(
    f"\n{'Model':<25} {'Count CV':>10} {'Count Test':>12} {'TFIDF CV':>10} {'TFIDF Test':>12}"
)
print("-" * 72)

for name, model in models.items():
    # CountVectorizer results
    cv_count = cross_val_score(
        model, X_train_count, y_train, cv=5, scoring="accuracy"
    ).mean()
    model.fit(X_train_count, y_train)
    test_count = accuracy_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test_count))

    # TF-IDF results
    cv_tfidf = cross_val_score(
        model, X_train_tfidf, y_train, cv=5, scoring="accuracy"
    ).mean()
    model.fit(X_train_tfidf, y_train)
    test_tfidf = accuracy_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test_tfidf))

    winner = "← TF-IDF wins!" if test_tfidf > test_count else ""
    print(
        f"{name:<25} {cv_count:>10.4f} {test_count:>12.4f} "
        f"{cv_tfidf:>10.4f} {test_tfidf:>12.4f} {winner}"
    )
```

sections.title: Step 6: Build Text Classification Pipeline
sections.body:
```python
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("TEXT CLASSIFICATION PIPELINE")
print("=" * 60)

# Best practice: put everything in a pipeline!
text_pipeline = Pipeline(
    [
        (
            "tfidf",
            TfidfVectorizer(
                max_features=10000,
                stop_words="english",
                min_df=2,
                max_df=0.95,
                ngram_range=(1, 2),
                sublinear_tf=True,
            ),
        ),
        ("classifier", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=42)),
    ]
)

# Train
text_pipeline.fit(X_train_text, y_train)
y_pred = text_pipeline.predict(X_test_text)

print(f"\nClassification Report:")
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred, target_names=target_names))
```

sections.title: Step 7: Visualization
sections.body:
```python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))

# Confusion Matrix
cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)
sns.heatmap(
    cm,
    annot=True,
    fmt="d",
    cmap="Blues",
    ax=axes[0],
    xticklabels=[n.split(".")[-1] for n in target_names],
    yticklabels=[n.split(".")[-1] for n in target_names],
)
axes[0].set_title("Confusion Matrix")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Predicted")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Actual")

# Count vs TF-IDF comparison
methods = ["Count", "TF-IDF"]
model_names_short = list(models.keys())
count_scores = []
tfidf_scores = []
for name, model in models.items():
    model.fit(X_train_count, y_train)
    count_scores.append(accuracy_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test_count)))
    model.fit(X_train_tfidf, y_train)
    tfidf_scores.append(accuracy_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test_tfidf)))

x = np.arange(len(model_names_short))
axes[1].bar(x - 0.2, count_scores, 0.35, label="CountVec", color="steelblue")
axes[1].bar(x + 0.2, tfidf_scores, 0.35, label="TF-IDF", color="coral")
axes[1].set_xticks(x)
axes[1].set_xticklabels(model_names_short, rotation=15)
axes[1].set_ylabel("Test Accuracy")
axes[1].set_title("CountVec vs TF-IDF")
axes[1].legend()

# Top words per category
tfidf_features = tfidf_vec.get_feature_names_out()
category_idx = 0  # sci.space
cat_mask = y_train == category_idx
mean_tfidf = X_train_tfidf[cat_mask].mean(axis=0).A1
top_idx = mean_tfidf.argsort()[-15:][::-1]
top_words_vals = [(tfidf_features[i], mean_tfidf[i]) for i in top_idx]
words, vals = zip(*top_words_vals)
axes[2].barh(range(len(words)), vals, color="steelblue")
axes[2].set_yticks(range(len(words)))
axes[2].set_yticklabels(words, fontsize=9)
axes[2].set_title(f"Top Words: {target_names[category_idx]}")
axes[2].invert_yaxis()

plt.suptitle("Text Classification Results", fontsize=16, fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("project_14_results.png", dpi=150)
plt.show()
```

sections.title: Step 8: Predict New Text
sections.body:
```python
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("PREDICTING NEW TEXT")
print("=" * 60)

new_texts = [
    "The NASA spacecraft landed on Mars successfully",
    "The pitcher threw a fastball for a strikeout",
    "The new GPU renders 3D graphics in real-time",
    "The new gun control legislation was debated in Congress",
]

predictions = text_pipeline.predict(new_texts)
proba = (
    text_pipeline.predict_proba(new_texts)
    if hasattr(text_pipeline, "predict_proba")
    else None
)

for text, pred in zip(new_texts, predictions):
    print(f"\n  Text: '{text}'")
    print(f"  Predicted: {target_names[pred]}")

# Save pipeline
joblib.dump(text_pipeline, "project_14_text_pipeline.pkl")
print("\n✓ Text pipeline saved!")

print(
    """
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║  KEY TAKEAWAYS - TEXT CLASSIFICATION                                ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                      ║
║  TEXT → NUMBERS:                                                     ║
║  • CountVectorizer: Simple word counts (Bag of Words)                ║
║  • TF-IDF: Weighted by importance (usually better!)                  ║
║  • ngram_range=(1,2): Captures bigrams like "machine learning"       ║
║                                                                      ║
║  KEY PARAMETERS:                                                     ║
║  • max_features: Vocabulary size (3000-50000)                        ║
║  • stop_words='english': Removes common words                       ║
║  • min_df / max_df: Filter very rare / very common words             ║
║  • ngram_range: (1,1)=unigrams, (1,2)=uni+bigrams                   ║
║  • sublinear_tf: Use log scaling (usually helps)                     ║
║                                                                      ║
║  BEST MODELS FOR TEXT:                                               ║
║  1. Logistic Regression (fast, good baseline)                        ║
║  2. Linear SVM (often best for text)                                 ║
║  3. Naive Bayes (fast, decent, great for small data)                 ║
║                                                                      ║
║  PIPELINE ADVANTAGE:                                                 ║
║  text_pipeline.predict(["new text"]) → works directly on text!       ║
║                                                                      ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
"""
)
```
